posts:
When political discourse collapses into weird anime fan fiction and sci-fi edits right before an election.
Evidence: Dept of Ed posts, Musk meme, Malfoid slang
#Aletheia #Culture #Politics

The online right framed pop-culture memes like Malfoid and Anakin Skywalker as relatable, engaging touchstones to connect with voters.

High-profile figures and agencies substituted bizarre internet subculture and incel-adjacent slang for actual policy substance.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.05, -0.05) — Greater Evil

- Playboy / Sosnick: PASS (+0.3, +0.2) — Sharp cultural critique of absurd online political theater.

Before the midterms, conservative accounts and official bodies like the Department of Education shared AI-generated Harry Potter and Star Wars memes.

The Poison:
Trading serious policy debates for niche internet memes alienates voters and trivializes the very institutions meant to serve them.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Plane Error (WHO/WHAT): Mistaking online engagement metrics for actual voter concern, treating fringe internet subcultures as mainstream politics.

Social Physics Analysis:
Actors run a superficial attention maneuver, replacing institutional transparency with viral memes to farm engagement without offering policy solutions.

The Trajectory: The Path of Fall into Destruction.
Modal Dynamics: can be -> Won't be via Regressive.
Trading constructive policy for internet memes reduces serious debate to performative noise.

The Unavoidable Truth: Internet subcultures now dictate public relations and political signaling.

The Unavoidable Lie: Memes substitute for substantive policy governance.

Actual Article Body:
Before the midterms, the right, including the Department of Education, devoted many political posts to Harry Potter and Star Wars.

This is The Manthropologist, a column by Charlie Sosnick about the Internet and the male mind.

Fresh off a midterm shellacking, Republicans will devote themselves to post-mortems and soul-searching, trying to understand what happened. If they are honest with themselves, they should acknowledge one crucial, bizarre mistake that largely flew under the radar: A week before Election Day, for no discernible reason, the online right devoted itself to posting Harry Potter and Star Wars fan fiction.

Leading up to Tuesday, conservative X accounts were obsessed with Malfoid, a gender-swapped Draco Malfoy, and dramatic edits of Anakin Skywalker. This reached some of the highest levels of the Trump administration, with the Department of Education posting AI art of both Malfoid and Anakin. “There’s magic in learning,” the caption reads. Palmer Luckey, founder of weapons contractor Anduril Industries and a leading tech voice on the right, posted a photo of him and his wife, Nicole Edelmann, dressed up as Harry and Malfoid for Halloween. Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, posted an AI-generated image of Anakin Skywalker with his wife and children, captioned “This is what they stole from you.”

For those of you not well-versed in Harry Potter fan fiction, Malfoid is one name for a common stock character. (The name is a portmanteau of Malfoy and “foid,” incel-derived internet slang for “woman.”) She is a female version of Draco Malfoy who falls in love with Harry. Great gobs of fan art depict Malfoid as a blond schoolgirl while retaining Draco’s cruel manner. The effect is something like an imaginary femdom girlfriend for thousands of adult men, who identify themselves as “sensitive young men” who are “yearning” for Malfoid. To those adult men, looking at anime girls on the computer constitutes a similar experience to wistfully thinking about your crush on a moonlit night.
